GETTING THERE

Base yourself in Kobuchizawa

🚄

Base yourself in Kobuchizawa or Chino and use a rental car to combine multiple resorts. Saku Ski Garden Parada is the exception — a 10-minute taxi from Sakudaira Shinkansen Station, making it ideal as a day trip directly from Tokyo. Most resorts are 30–60 minutes from Kobuchizawa Station by car.

SKI AREAS

The hidden gems

Quieter, drier, and more authentic — these seven resorts offer excellent skiing without the crowds that define the more famous destinations.

Takamine Mountain Park

高峰マウンテンパーク

¥3,800/day
300m Vertical
2000m Summit
12 Runs
5 Lifts
4 green
5 blue
2 red
1 black
🪑 3 chairlift 🎿 2 surface

One of the highest ski areas in the entire region, with a base altitude of 1,700 m and a summit touching 2,000 m — the same elevation as some Hakuba peaks. The high altitude brings exceptionally dry, cold powder that lasts well into March. Perched on the flanks of active Asama Volcano, clear days reward skiers with a surreal panorama of the volcano's crater rim and the Yatsugatake range beyond. A compact mountain, mostly intermediate terrain, with surprisingly few crowds even on peak weekends.

Snowmaking Dec – Mar
💡

Arrive early — the high elevation means morning fog rolls in frequently around 10:00. First tracks on a bluebird morning here are spectacular.

Yachiho Kogen Ski Resort

八千穂高原スキー場

¥3,200/day
250m Vertical
1650m Summit
9 Runs
5 Lifts
3 green
4 blue
2 red
🪑 3 chairlift 🎿 2 surface

A peaceful highland ski area set among the birch forests of Minamimaki at 1,400 m. No snowmaking means 100% natural snow — when it falls, the quality is outstanding. The gentle terrain and low visitor numbers make this a favourite among locals who want to avoid the Golden Week crowds at larger resorts. The larch and birch trees that line the runs are magnificent in mid-winter, especially after a fresh snowfall turns them silver-white. One of the best-value resorts in the entire Yatsugatake region.

Dec – Mar
💡

Check snow reports before visiting — no snowmaking means conditions depend entirely on recent snowfall. After a good dump, this place is magical.

Chateraise Ski Valley Nobeyama

シャトレーゼスキーバレー野辺山

¥3,000/day
155m Vertical
1500m Summit
11 Runs
5 Lifts
5 green
4 blue
2 red
🪑 3 chairlift 🟫 2 magic carpet

Operated by the beloved Japanese confectionery company Chateraise, this highland resort sits near the famous Nobeyama Radio Observatory at one of the highest base elevations in the Yatsugatake area. The terrain is gentle and perfectly suited to families and beginners, with wide groomed runs and very patient instructors. Magic carpet lifts mean children can ski their first runs without wrestling chairlifts. A wonderful introduction to Japanese ski culture — low-key, welcoming, and reasonably priced.

Snowmaking Dec – early Mar
💡

The base lodge sells Chateraise cakes and ice cream year-round — a uniquely Japanese ski break. The strawberry shortcake après-ski is practically mandatory.

The smaller of the two Chateraise-operated resorts, Koumi Ski Valley sits near the Koumi Line railway and offers the most affordable skiing in the entire region. The compact layout with wide, gentle slopes is ideal for first-timers and young children taking their first ski lessons. The Koumi area's rural character — surrounded by farmhouses and cedar forests — gives it a charming, off-the-beaten-track feel that the larger resorts can't replicate. A genuine hidden gem for families on a budget.

Snowmaking Dec – Feb
💡

Pair a morning here with an afternoon visit to Nobeyama for a good variety of terrain in a single day. The 20-minute drive between the two resorts is quick.

Fujimi Kogen Ski Resort

富士見高原スキー場

¥4,200/day
450m Vertical
1450m Summit
10 Runs
5 Lifts
3 green
4 blue
3 red
🚡 1 gondola 🪑 3 chairlift 🎿 1 surface

Not to be confused with Fujimi Panorama Resort next door — Fujimi Kogen is a distinct mountain with its own gondola and character. The gondola offers panoramic views across the Suwa basin and on clear days reaches all the way to the Pacific coast. The resort attracts a mix of beginners and intermediates, with long groomed blue runs dominating the upper mountain. The access is excellent — just a 10-minute taxi from JR Fujimi Station on the Chuo Line, making it one of the easiest resorts to reach without a rental car.

Snowmaking Dec – Mar
💡

Take the gondola to the summit for a clear-day view across to the Pacific. The top-to-bottom blue run is the longest uninterrupted groomed run in the area.

Saku Ski Garden Parada

佐久スキーガーデン パラダ

¥4,500/day
400m Vertical
1400m Summit
14 Runs
6 Lifts
4 green
5 blue
3 red
2 black
🚡 1 gondola 🪑 4 chairlift 🎿 1 surface

The most Tokyo-accessible ski resort in the Yatsugatake region — Sakudaira Shinkansen Station is just 10 minutes away, meaning you can be on snow within 90 minutes of leaving central Tokyo. Despite the easy access, Parada punches well above its weight: a gondola, 400 m vertical, night skiing until 21:00, and a proper terrain park. The long blue runs from the summit are ideal for developing skiers, and the night skiing adds a completely different dimension for afternoon arrivals from Tokyo. A favourite for Tokyo office workers doing a ski day mid-week.

Night skiing Snowmaking Terrain park Dec – Mar
💡

Take the 07:30 Hokuriku Shinkansen from Tokyo to Sakudaira — you'll be on snow by 09:30. A mid-week day trip is perfectly doable and avoids weekend crowds.

Eight Peaks Resort

¥3,500/day
250m Vertical
1750m Summit
7 Runs
3 Lifts
2 green
3 blue
2 red
🪑 2 chairlift 🎿 1 surface

A boutique resort sitting high on the Yatsugatake range at 1,500 m, Eight Peaks is the closest ski area to Kobuchizawa and the most intimate option in the region. The name refers to the eight peaks of the Yatsugatake volcano group visible from the summit. No snowmaking and a shorter season mean the conditions are entirely weather-dependent, but on good snow days the natural terrain and the absence of crowds create an experience that feels miles away from the commercial resorts. Popular with powder enthusiasts who know the area well.

Dec – late Feb
💡

Follow the resort on social media for real-time snow updates — they post daily conditions. Only come on a confirmed powder day for the best experience.

AND IF YOU WANT THE CROWDS

Hakuba Valley

World-class terrain — but Hakuba is one of Japan's most internationally recognised ski destinations. Expect lift queues, premium pricing, and fully booked accommodation during peak season. Listed last intentionally: explore the Yatsugatake region first.

Hakuba Valley

白馬バレー

¥6,500/day
1071m Vertical
1831m Summit
99 Runs
55 Lifts
15 green
40 blue
25 red
19 black
🚡 5 gondola 🪑 38 chairlift 🎿 12 surface

The crown jewel of Japanese skiing — and the most crowded. Hakuba Valley links 10 interconnected resorts (including Happo-one, Goryu, and Tsugaike) across 1,071 m of vertical, making it one of the largest ski areas in Asia. The international ski community is deeply rooted here since the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics, and the village has a thriving English-speaking expat scene. The terrain is genuinely world-class and the snowfall is legendary. However, peak season (late December through February) sees enormous crowds — long lift queues, fully booked restaurants, and accommodation prices to match. Listed last for a reason: explore the quieter Yatsugatake-area resorts first, and save Hakuba for when you want the full-scale experience.

Night skiing Snowmaking Terrain park Nov – May
💡

If you go, aim for March — the snowpack is still excellent, the crowds thin significantly, and accommodation prices drop. Avoid Christmas week and early February at all costs.
